text.p: The following are the main stories from Monday morning's German newspapers:

- Coalition government and opposition SPD to start talks today on tax reform. Chancellor Helmut Kohl warns against turning talks into platform for party politics. SPD leader Rudolf Scharping doesn't expect quick agreement.

- Research Minister Ruettgers presents his plan for reform of universities and say plan should pass through parliament this year. Proposal would reduce students time in universities and give universities power to select students.
- Group of CDU politicians want to push federal government to begin issuing debt titles in euro rather than marks on January 1, 1999.
- German rail denies reports that it plans to shut down thousands of kilometres of unprofitable rail lines.
- Kohl says parts of tax reform could be implemented in 1998. CDU, FDP and SPD signal willingness to compromise on eve of meetings on tax reform in Bonn.
- OeTV union leader makes new offer to help job creation. Herbert Mai, chairman of OeTV, says it may be possible to reduce working hours without full pay compensation.
- Health Minister Horst Seehofer comes under pressure over his proposal to raise health insurance fees.
- Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel appeals for early entry into EU for Czech Republic.

- CDU parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaeuble raises questions about the social system in Germany, saying people have to have more faith in their own abilities again rather than relying heavily on state.
- Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt succumbs to pressure from eastern German states and western German towns and agrees to protect brown coal industry from competition until year 2003.
- Finance Minister Theo Waigel says painful cuts are necessary. Coalition hopeful that tax reform meeting with SPD will lead to turnaround on jobs market.
- Tough fight ahead for health care reform.
